Uncle Cranky Pants on Owning a House

I'm almost 50 now and wish I'd known this stuff sooner. I don't remember an adult saying these things to me when I was a kid, so I'm saying them here in the hopes it helps someone else.

Owning a house costs much more than the monthly (principal+interest+insurance+taxes) payment

A house needs constant upkeep or that thing will break down around you. Esimates in 2020 say to budget about $1000 per year on upkeep. But when you buy a house it's likely to need a bunch of stuff fairly quickly.

We bought our most recent house four years ago. The refrigerator, microwave, dishwasher, and heat pump/A.C. unit all went out. The range is on its last legs.

We had to replace every last light switch and electrical outlet in the house, showers heads, sinks, faucets, and all the lights in the garage/workshop. We did maintenance on the garage roof ourselves. The house roof will need replacement in the next year or two, estimated cost $7000-$10,000. That's in addition to yard work, cleaning off the roof, and minor repairs everywhere.

We haven't even had a chance to address cosmetic, feel-good things like replacing the moss lawn with grass or painting the interior.

When we were renting, we made less money and it was easy to build savings. Money went to stuff we wanted instead of maintenance. Everything just worked. I deeply miss the financial freedom, lack of maintenance, and lack of worry that came with renting.

House ownership builds equity, but equity sucks

What is equity?

It's money you paid on mortgage principal that you don't have access to any more. Instead of that money being in your account, it belongs to a bank.

Rising house prices also create equity. That's not a huge win because selling your house at an inflated price means buying your next house at an inflated price. You won't see a dime of that money unless you sell your house and go back to renting

Equity has an opportunity cost. Money you pay into equity is money you can't use to start a business, invest elsewhere, or spend on a better life now.

Equity isn't completely useless:

* You can use a home equity loan to get even more debt

* It can help you buy a nicer house when you move

* It's a potential inheritance for your kids/family

Actually paying off your house is . . . unlikely

Our parents in both families had lifetimes of good income and careful money management. Both are now in their 80s. One side still pays mortgage on the house every month. The other just paid it off a few months ago. They have lived in a bank-owned houses their entire lives.

If you never need a home equity loan, never refinance, never have to move, and never miss a payment, your home will be paid off in 30 years. Good luck.

Owning a house versus renting isn't a clear-cut choice

We have bought very modest houses twice. Both times our standard of living dropped and we were broke for years afterwards. The house wages a constant war with our bank account. Having savings means living with stuff that's broken. It sucks.

When we rented, we were making less money and it was easy to build savings. Extra money went to stuff we wanted, not maintenance. We lived in better places with more perks than we have as house "owners". And we were free to move when needed for job changes.

Your situation may work out differently. I'm not saying buy or don't buy. But don't feel bad if you're still renting. There are pros and cons to both sides.
